summary: Updates the RTP payload format for the G.729.1 audio codec to add discontinuous transmission, which skips sending packets during silence, in a backward-compatible way. It updates RFC 4749 and includes an updated media type registration. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When nobody is talking, you don't need to send sound. This update lets the phone stay quiet during pauses, saving bandwidth.

subtitle: How G.729.1 voice over RTP can stay quiet during pauses in speech, without breaking older receivers.

tldr.problem: G.729.1 supports Discontinuous Transmission (DTX), or silence suppression, but the RTP payload format in RFC 4749 had no way to carry the small silence frames that DTX produces.
tldr.mechanism: The update lets a Silence Insertion Descriptor (SID) ride at the end of a payload or alone with frame type 14, sets the Marker bit on the first packet of a talkspurt, and adds a negotiable dtx parameter.
tldr.outcome: Senders can stop transmitting during silence and receivers can generate comfort noise. The change is binary backward-compatible with RFC 4749, which this RFC updates.

facts.label: Marker bit
facts.value: 1 on first packet of a talkspurt

today: RFC 5459 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4749. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
ITU-T Recommendation G.729.1 is a scalable and wideband extension of the G.729 audio codec. RFC 4749 defines how G.729.1 audio is packed into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

Annex C of G.729.1 adds Discontinuous Transmission (DTX) to the codec. This RFC updates the RTP payload format so that Annex C can be used. It describes only changes or additions to RFC 4749, so the two documents are read together.
sections.plainLanguage: There was already a rule book for sending this kind of voice over the internet. This note adds a few new pages about what to do during quiet moments.

sections.title: DTX, SID and Comfort Noise
sections.content:
DTX is also known as silence suppression. The coder includes a Voice Activity Detection (VAD) algorithm that decides whether an audio frame holds silence or actual audio. During silence the coder may greatly reduce the transmitted bit rate by sending a small frame called a Silence Insertion Descriptor (SID) and then stopping transmission.

The receiver's decoder generates comfort noise (CNG) from the parameters in the SID. The G.729.1 SID has an embedded structure: the core SID is the same as the legacy G.729 SID, a first enhancement layer adds parameters for narrowband comfort noise, and a second adds wideband information. A G.729.1 SID can be 2, 3, or 6 octets long.
sections.plainLanguage: When you stop talking, the phone sends one tiny note describing the background hum. The other phone then plays a similar hum so the line does not sound dead.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage and the Marker Bit
sections.content:
The RTP header fields are used as described in RFC 4749, except for the Marker (M) bit. If DTX is used, the first packet of a talkspurt MUST have the M bit set to 1. A talkspurt starts with the first packet after a silence period during which packets were not transmitted contiguously. The M bit in all other packets MUST be 0.

The start of a talkspurt MAY be used to adjust the playout delay to reflect changing network delays. If DTX is not used, the M bit MUST be 0 in all packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The first packet after a pause waves a little flag so the listener knows someone started talking again.

sections.title: Payload Format with a SID
sections.content:
The payload format is that of RFC 4749 with the option to add a SID at the end. A complete payload is a 1-octet payload header (the MBS and FT fields), then zero or more audio frames at the same bit rate, then zero or one SID. This is consistent with the G.729 payload format in section 4.5.6 of RFC 3551.

To send a SID alone, the frame type value FT=14 is assigned to the SID. With FT=14, only a single SID SHALL be included, and its size (2, 3, or 6 octets) is inferred from the payload size. When a SID follows audio frames, FT keeps describing the audio encoding rate. The SID is much smaller than any audio frame, so the receiver can detect it and the frame count is not disturbed.

Section 5.4 of RFC 4749 told receivers to ignore bytes left after complete frames. This RFC overrides that: the remainder is treated as a SID. If its size is not 2, 3, or 6 octets, the receiver MUST ignore those bytes. DTX has no impact on the definition and use of MBS.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet can carry a little extra note at the end, or the note can travel alone in its own packet. The receiver tells which by how big the packet is.

sections.title: The dtx Parameter and SDP
sections.content:
Parameters from RFC 4749 are not modified. One new optional parameter is added to the audio/G7291 media subtype: dtx, with permissible values 0 and 1. A value of 0 means no DTX and 1 means DTX support as in Annex C of G.729.1. If the parameter is omitted, 0 is implied. When DTX is off, the payload MUST NOT contain a SID and FT value 14 MUST NOT be used.

In the Session Description Protocol (SDP), the parameter goes in the a=fmtp attribute. The RFC's second example offers a 40 ms packet duration, a maximum bit rate of 20 kbps, and DTX supported and preferred.

Offer-answer rules

Both directions must use the same DTX setting. DTX is active if, and only if, dtx=1 appears in both the offer and the answer. For multicast the parameter is declarative and MUST NOT be negotiated.

A receiver that follows only RFC 4749 ignores dtx and leaves it out of its answer, so DTX is not activated. Such a receiver would not be confused by a DTX stream, but during silence it would use packet loss concealment instead of comfort noise, giving bad audio. This is why the parameter exists despite binary backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Both phones must agree before going quiet during pauses. If either one does not understand the new feature, nobody uses it.

sections.title: Congestion and Security
sections.content:
The congestion control considerations of RFC 4749 apply. DTX can help by reducing the number of RTP packets sent and the average bandwidth of audio streams.

The security considerations of RFC 4749 also apply. By watching an RTP flow that uses DTX, an attacker could see when and for how long people are speaking. The RFC calls this a general fact about DTX and says G.729.1 DTX introduces no new specific issue.
sections.plainLanguage: Going quiet saves room on the network. But someone watching could tell when you are talking, because packets only flow then.
